item.title: US aircraft carrier docks near Thai beach resort Pattaya after record 250 days at sea
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cg7k09z4lj9o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
US aircraft carrier docks near Thai beach resort Pattaya after record 250 days at sea - Published After a record 250 days at sea without a port stop, the nuclear-powered aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln has docked in Thailand, giving its nearly 5,000 crew members a much-needed break. The ship is docking close to the beach resort of Pattaya, known for its raucous nightlife and for sex tourism. For the US it also carries strong historical echoes. When the weary sailors walk into the city's bars and restaurants, they will literally be treading in the footsteps of the hundreds of thousands of US troops who came here for R&R – rest and relaxation - during the Vietnam War. They transformed it from a sleepy fishing village to one of the world's most famous and frenetic party towns. Today the neon-lit alleys running down to the beach are much quieter than usual. The bars in the city's famous Walking Street still screen videos on their walls of pole-dancing women, trying to lure customers inside. But there are not many of those customers, and most seem to be family groups from the Middle East more interested in the Turkish ice-cream vendor than the go-go bars. The Iran War, which has affected tourism and consumer spending, has hit businesses hard here. The prospect of thousands of American sailors, with nine months of salary unspent while at sea, offers a rare opportunity to local businesses. The US carrier left San Diego last November on what was supposed to be a six-month assignment in the Pacific and South China Sea. However, the ship was diverted to the Gulf after the US and Israel began military operations against Iran in late February. Recently some members of Congress raised concern about reports of food shortages, broken toilets and mental stress among the crew. The US Navy acknowledged that working conditions have been tough, but said the crew were sufficiently well-supported. It would not, however, comment to the BBC on the carrier docking at Pattaya, citing operational security. Despite its close relationship with China, Thailand is a treaty ally of the US, and port visits by US Navy ships are a familiar occurrence. But this is probably the largest number of US military personnel coming straight from a war zone to Pattaya since the fall of Saigon in 1975. "This visit could be our best hope," said Anon Saiteer, who sells gems in a shop near Walking Street, which has put up a large sign welcoming the US sailors and marines and offering them a special discount. "We have nothing to lose – we just hope they will spend some money here." But US and Thai officials are trying to ensure this happens without any of the salacious headlines for which Pattaya has become known. The Thai authorities have said there are a few places where the US servicemen and women will not be allowed to go. One of them is Soi 6, which runs down to the main beach, and is known for its concentration of racy go-go bars. While the Thai police have reminded their US visitors that prostitution is technically illegal in Thailand, there are actually thought to be 25,000 to 50,000 sex workers in the city. Many of them work in Soi 6, where they stand outside the bars imploring men to come inside. The many cannabis shops in Pattaya are also off-limits to US crew members, along with sea-sports like paragliding and jet-skis. "It is their decision," Mayor Poramase Ngampiches told the BBC. "The US military have done their homework." US Naval Attache Kristopher Robinson rebuffed questions from the BBC about activities that soldiers were banned from doing. Instead, he said the US troops would "conduct themselves in accordance with US law, US naval regulations, and the laws of Thailand". "We're trying to give the sailors as much opportunity for rest as they can," he said. The US Navy has organised shuttle buses from the port into Pattaya running from 5am to 2am every day the carrier is here in Thailand. Two hotels have been designated suitable for those US crew members who want to splash out on a night onshore. The Thai authorities have deployed hundreds of police officers to keep an eye on the city's entertainment zones, and warned local businesses not to overcharge their American guests. "The visits of US military men 50-60 years ago introduced Pattaya to the world and turned it into a tourist attraction," says Mayor Poramase. "We have to be frank, the city has a reputation for bar girls. We understand the stereotypes. We can't stop that. "What we can do is to show that Pattaya has changed, that we now have other things, such as sports, seminars, wellness and family-friendly activities. It's a mixture of everything." Both countries hope that by the time the USS Abraham Lincoln begins the long journey home across the Pacific on 6 September, it will be with a refreshed and rested crew. With additional reporting from Nongnapat Patcham.

item.title: Thousands still missing as Nepal-Tibet flood relief and recovery intensifies
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8xk45k9r1go?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Thousands still missing as Nepal-Tibet flood relief and recovery intensifies - Published Thousands of people remain missing after a catastrophic flash flood along the Nepal-Tibet border a week ago, as rescuers scramble to reach anyone who may be alive even as they turn to recovery. At least 1,114 people have died in Nepal and nearly 4,000 more are missing, according to Nepal's disaster agency. On the Tibetan side, the death toll stands at 16, and more than 500 people are unaccounted for, Chinese state media reports. The UN's humanitarian agency has said the response is entering a new phase, with authorities intensifying relief and recovery operations. In Nepal, efforts continue to rescue workers, potentially in the hundreds, believed to be trapped in hydroelectric station tunnels. A massive flash flood, believed to have been triggered by a glacial collapse, swept through a Himalayan valley last Wednesday, wiping out villages. Nearly 12,000 people have since been rescued, according to Nepal's disaster management agency. But thousands more, including hundreds of foreign nationals - from India, the UK, Australia, the US, Malaysia, and more - are still missing. A week on, fears are growing that the death toll will only rise. Chinese state media has not reported any survivors on the Tibetan side of the border, but the search continues. Beijing, which annexed Tibet in the 1950s, tightly controls the region. All information comes from state media and foreign journalists cannot travel there without permission. Rescuers using heavy machinery, working around the clock, have been able to re-open the route to the Gyirong border crossing between Nepal and Tibet and clear the road of debris, which will accelerate the search for the missing, Chinese state media said. Rescue operations continue in challenging conditions, and experts from China and India are helping build temporary bridges to reach remote areas. Drones are being deployed over hard-to reach areas to scan for survivors. The UN's humanitarian agency said the main challenge is now access, with more than 40 bridges destroyed. The most remote communities are relying on army helicopter flights for supplies, and villages are still struggling for fuel and electricity. The full impact of the flood in Tibet is unclear. China has released information through state media outlets showing the devastation around the border, but has given few details about the victims or the impact on local villagers. In Nepal, nearly 3,500 people have been left homeless and displaced in 27 sites - mostly schools, which disrupts education - across the districts of Nuwakot and Rasuwa. The priority for them now is "receiving humanitarian assistance, recovering and identifying the remains of the loved ones, tracing missing relatives and reunifying separated children, and accessing psychosocial support", the UN's humanitarian agency said. People packed into overcrowded shelters, contaminated water and damaged health facilities are putting the population at greater risk of disease in the middle of the monsoon season, the agency added. Nepal's prime minister, Balendra Shah, said there was a renewed emphasis on protecting the lives of survivors, providing medical treatment and psychological counselling. Nepal's government and the UN have agreed to launch a four-month humanitarian flash appeal. - Published18 hours ago - Published1 day ago

item.title: BBC travels inside occupied Lebanon as officials say Israel expanding positions
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cge41d19gq9o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
BBC travels inside occupied Lebanon as officials say Israel expanding positions - Published The drive on the highway by the Mediterranean in southern Lebanon, near the border with Israel, is scenic and, these days, desolate. Crops lie abandoned and buildings destroyed by Israeli air strikes, too many to count, are in ruins. Near the town of Naqoura, a Lebanese military checkpoint, painted in the white-and-red colours of the national flag, is the last visible sign of the state's presence. Soldiers are positioned behind concrete walls, but the road is empty. A few minutes further south, around a dozen Israeli flags indicate the start of occupied territory. Unless authorised by Israel, no-one can enter. This part of the country is the heartland of Lebanon's Shia Muslim community, from which Hezbollah, the Iranian-backed militia and political party, gets most of its support. It has seen three invasions by the Israeli military in wars against the group in the last two decades alone. The most recent started in March, after Hezbollah fired rockets into Israel following the killing of the Iranian supreme leader, at the start of the US and Israel's war against Iran. Last month, a BBC team joined a humanitarian mission of the UN peacekeeping force in Lebanon, known as Unifil, which is one of the only ways to visit the area under Israeli control. There, as it did in Gaza, Israel has flattened entire villages, and air strikes and demolitions have continued even after a ceasefire was announced in June. Led by Finnish troops who are part of Unifil, the convoy was escorting civilians to and from Christian villages near the border. Those communities were spared from Israel's attacks and invasion during the war and, with the surrounding areas now under occupation, are now cut off from the rest of the country. Our presence was allowed by the Israeli military through a deconfliction mechanism with the UN. The strip of land currently controlled by Israel constitutes around 5% of Lebanese territory and, in some places, extends 10km (six miles) from the border. Driving along the wall that separates the two countries, we saw service roads built by Israel after the invasion, intense movement of Israeli soldiers and residential buildings that were being used by them. Some were covered in netting to protect them from Hezbollah's explosive drones. We also heard Israeli surveillance drones in the sky and explosions in the distance, possibly from demolitions being carried out by Israel in villages that are under occupation. In a visit to occupied southern Lebanon last month, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said he had instructed the military to "take all necessary steps to prepare for a long-term presence in the area". Israeli officials say their goal is to establish what they call a "security zone" to protect communities in northern Israel from rockets and drones that have been fired by Hezbollah from southern Lebanon, as well as a possible ground invasion. According to Unifil, the Israeli military has established four new bases in the invaded areas, bringing the number of such positions to nine. Israeli forces had remained in five points after invading southern Lebanon during the previous war against Hezbollah in 2024, in violation of the deal that ended that conflict. "In the past months, we've seen the consolidation and fortification of Israeli positions, construction of protective infrastructure, and other engineering works," Kandice Ardiel, a Unifil spokeswoman, said. "We have [also] observed what appear to be Israeli civilian personnel carrying out demolition and engineering activities in support of military activities in south Lebanon." Human rights groups say some of Israel's actions in southern Lebanon amount to the deliberate destruction of civilian infrastructure, a possible war crime. Hundreds of thousands of Lebanese remain displaced, without knowing when, or if, they will be able to return. In response to our questions, the Israeli military said the buildings that had been destroyed were used by Hezbollah for military purposes, and that it operated in accordance with international law. It did not respond to other specific questions about its actions in the occupied areas. In June, the US and Iran announced a preliminary deal aimed at ending their conflict, which included a cessation of the violence in Lebanon. Since then, a Lebanese intelligence official told me, Lebanon's military has recorded more than 5,000 violations of the deal by Israel, including air strikes, drone attacks, shelling and near-daily incursions of Israeli soldiers into Lebanese territory beyond the area under occupation, the so-called Yellow Line. As it does in Gaza, the Israeli military justifies some of its attacks in Lebanon as operations against what it describes as immediate threats. In many cases, however, it is not clear how immediate these alleged threats are or if there is any threat at all. Hezbollah, which is considered a terrorist organisation by countries including the UK and the US, has not carried out attacks against Israel since the ceasefire came into force, but has targeted Israeli troops operating inside Lebanese territory. "[The Israelis] are expanding their presence [in Lebanon]. They've [also] been setting areas ablaze, demolishing houses while the bombing continues, despite the ceasefire," the Lebanese intelligence official said. "It's clear that they don't want anyone to go back [to those villages] in the coming year, or even years. This isn't only about Hezbollah. This is about preventing people from returning." Israeli officials have conditioned a withdrawal from Lebanon on Hezbollah's disarmament, something the Lebanese government cannot deliver without the group's consent. Hezbollah, observers say, is still a significant military force despite the setbacks in the recent wars. Both countries have held direct talks that resulted in a framework agreement brokered by the US: Israel would pull out of certain areas, called "pilot zones", where Lebanese army soldiers would be deployed and Hezbollah's disarmament would be verified. Hezbollah opposes the efforts – the group's leader, Naim Qassem, called them "surrender with humiliation" last week – and says any discussion about its weapons should only happen after a full Israeli withdrawal. Israel, for its part, has claimed that the Lebanese national military, which rejects the use of force against the group saying this could pit Lebanese against Lebanese, has not done enough. The plan has seen no progress, and there is no expectation of any significant change before the Israeli election at the end of October. "The idea of the 'pilot zones' seems to be dead until the context changes," a European diplomat familiar with the situation told me. "It seems we're heading to a Gaza-like situation. The Israelis are entrenching themselves... and are here to stay, for now." - Published15 August - Published6 August

item.title: Zelensky says airlines should avoid Russian airspace as Ukraine escalates drone operations
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9v9yydy2wvo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Zelensky says airlines should avoid Russian airspace as Ukraine escalates drone operations - Published Ukraine's president has told airlines that Russian airspace will be "effectively closing" as his country escalates its drone strikes. "We want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, everyone who still uses key Russian airports: the Russian sky is becoming completely dangerous," Volodymyr Zelensky said. Russian President Vladimir Putin responded by saying that Zelensky's comments amounted to a "declaration of state terrorism". Russia, he added, would continue its attacks on Ukraine which have intensified in recent weeks. Most Western commercial airlines do not fly over Russia as a consequence of the ongoing Russian invasion of Ukraine, but carriers in countries such as Turkey and China do. Explaining the elevated airspace risk in his nightly video address on Tuesday, Zelensky said that "Ukraine does not threaten civilian aviation as such - not a single civilian aircraft" and did not want the loss of innocent lives. "There will simply be drones in Russia's skies on a scale that has to be taken into account," he said. Zelensky directed the warning to airlines continuing to operate flights to Russian airports, especially in major cities like St Petersburg and Moscow. Ukraine has targeted energy facilities deep inside Russian territory and there have been repeated attacks on depots belonging to Russia's two biggest online retailers, Wildberries and Ozon. Its drone attacks have for months led to disruption at some of Russia's biggest airports, especially in Moscow where at times all four major airports have been forced to halt arrivals and departures. Several cancellations were reported on Wednesday. Ukraine does not have to target airports to cause disruption. Under Russia's air defence "Kovyor" (carpet) plan, flights are suspended if a drone is detected in the relevant area. Aviation risk advisory firm Osprey Flight Solutions said in an alert to clients that while the majority of Ukraine's drone and missile strikes were likely to occur within 300km (186 miles) of the border, daily attacks deeper inside Russia were almost certain to continue this year. "There is also a realistic possibility that the frequency of Ukrainian strikes will continue to increase in the short term deep inside Russian territory," the alert added. "It is assessed that miscalculation and/or misidentification is likely in areas related to the Ukraine conflict." Speaking to reporters at the Shanghai Co-operation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan, Putin said: "They are asking us to resume negotiations... but you don't negotiate with terrorists." His comments come as Russia's attacks on Ukraine continue, with heavy strikes killing 12 people on Tuesday and further attacks on Odesa, Sumy and Kyiv on Wednesday. Russia's military has said it is preparing to carry out "massive" strikes on Ukrainian power stations. The Ukrainian capital and its surrounding region have come under attack for seven days in a row. A few weeks ago, Zelensky said Russia was attacking Ukraine every day, and Ukraine's military had "begun the process of bringing the war back to Russia". At the weekend he said the same, that Russia had to feel the war was "returning to where it came from". Putin acknowledged that Ukrainian strikes had damaged infrastructure inside Russia, while insisting that "only 10%" of oil refineries were left to repair. Chinese, Turkish and Gulf state airlines are among those using Russian airspace, with savings in time and fuel on routes between Asia and Europe. Other carriers have largely avoided the eastern European region since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion in February, 2022. Ukraine has closed its airspace to civilian aircraft throughout that period. The risks of civil aviation during a war are clear. A few months after war broke out in eastern Ukraine in 2014 between Russian-backed separatists and the Ukrainian military, a Russian-made missile brought down a passenger plane, killing all 298 people on board. Last year, the UN aviation agency ruled that Russia was responsible for the downing of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17 over eastern Ukraine in July 2014. The Kremlin has always denied any responsibility for the air disaster. In 2024, Putin apologised to the president of neighbouring Azerbaijan over the downing of a commercial airliner in Russian airspace, in which 38 people were killed. He said the "tragic incident" had occurred when Russian air defence systems were repelling Ukrainian drones. Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Bus crash on Egypt's Red Sea coast kills 16 - Published At least 16 people have been killed in a bus crash in eastern Egypt, the country's health ministry has said. Another 28 people were injured on the road between Red Sea towns of Dahab and Nuweiba in the South Sinai governorate on Wednesday morning. Reports in Egyptian and Jordanian media say Jordanian nationals were among those killed in the accident. As many as 20 ambulances were sent to the crash scene to provide first aid and evacuate the injured, the Egyptian health ministry said. The cause of the crash remains unknown. The area is a popular tourist destination, attracting visitors from around the world. Deadly road accidents are common across Egypt, with the authorities reporting nearly 6,000 fatalities in 2025. Such accidents are often blamed on reckless driving and poor road maintenance. Last month, 18 people were killed and 30 injured when two lorries collided in the north-eastern Ismailia governorate.

item.title: Charlie Kirk murder suspect pleads not guilty as judge clears way for death penalty trial
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj4jn9q7evpo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Charlie Kirk murder suspect pleads not guilty as judge clears way for death penalty trial - Published A 23-year-old Utah man has pleaded not guilty to the murder of conservative activist Charlie Kirk – as a judge ruled prosecutors can seek the death penalty at trial. Tyler Robinson denies aggravated murder, a capital offence in Utah, and six other charges in connection with the shooting of Kirk at a campus event on 10 September 2025. Defence lawyers had tried to have the death penalty taken off the table, but prosecutors argued that aggravating factors, such as firing into a crowd in the presence of children, warranted a capital trial. Turning Point USA co-founder Kirk, 31, was shot in the neck while speaking at Utah Valley University in Orem. The defendant, wearing a grey suit and occasionally consulting with his lawyers, appeared in court in the city of Provo on Tuesday. Kirk's widow, Erika, the mother of their two children, and his parents, Robert and Kathryn, were also at the hearing. In a statement shared afterwards, the Kirk family said the judge's decision "marks an important step" in their "pursuit of justice". "Every step in this process carries the weight of all that Charlie's murder has taken from his family, especially his children who will grow up without their father," the statement added. Closing arguments followed a five-day preliminary hearing in July, during which prosecutors outlined their evidence to show probable cause for trial. That included DNA allegedly tying Robinson to the murder weapon and other items recovered at the scene; confessions he allegedly made to loved ones; and a taped video statement from his roommate and romantic partner, Lance Twiggs. "There is a mountain of evidence that proves that he is the shooter," prosecutor Ryan McBride told the court on Tuesday, outlining video that he said showed Robinson "dressed to kill" on campus on the day of the shooting. "We know that the defendant is the shooter… first, because of the video evidence; second, because of the DNA; third, because of his admissions; and fourth, because of circumstantial evidence," McBride said. Prosecutors said the accused, a former apprentice electrician, was in a relationship with his roommate and regarded Kirk's conservative views, particularly on transgender issues, as "repugnant" - which they argued was the motive. On Tuesday, prosecutors also outlined "aggravating" factors - accusing the defendant of "gambling with the lives of others" when he allegedly fired towards Kirk, who was surrounded by other people. "He was playing, in effect, a game of ballistic roulette," prosecutor Chad Grunander said. "It's been 356 days since Tyler Robinson assassinated Charlie Kirk," Grunander added. "It's time for him, the defendant, to be bound over for trial and arraigned. Today." Defence lawyers attempted to sow doubt about the prosecution's evidence. During July's hearing, they raised questions about procedure and the credentials of experts who testified. Robinson's lawyers have repeatedly objected to cameras livestreaming court proceedings. Judge Tony Graf again listened to arguments on the issue during a sealed hearing on Tuesday morning before closing arguments began - but he ruled in favour of transparency in a case that has sparked conspiracy theories. On Tuesday, the defence sought to downplay the aggravating factors outlined by prosecutors - arguing that no bullets hit anyone in the crowd apart from Kirk. Who Was Charlie Kirk? Conservative activist Charlie Kirk was shot dead in Utah. But what shaped his views and how did he rise to become one of the most important right-wing influencers in the United States? The court heard and saw during July's hearing how the accused allegedly scouted the campus repeatedly on the day Kirk was shot - interacting with TPUSA members and eating Chick-fil-A before returning in different clothes. The new outfit included "long pants to obscure the rifle he had concealed down his pants", McBride said on Tuesday. According to prosecutors' evidence presented during the July hearing, Robinson's DNA was found on his grandfather's rifle stashed in a wooden area near campus after the shooting, as well as on a towel it was wrapped in and a screwdriver recovered at the scene. McBride also told the court on Tuesday that engravings found on casings from the shooting allegedly matched a Dremel tool recovered at the home the defendant shared with his roommate. Twiggs' videotaped interview with prosecutors was played in July during the hearing. Robinson's roommate testified that the defendant had confessed to the shooting, cried and said he wished he hadn't done it. Robinson, in the company of his family and a neighbour, turned himself in the day after the murder. He is next due in court on 23 October, when a trial date is expected to be set.

item.title: South Korea jails care home head for sexually assaulting disabled residents
item.description:

========================================
South Korea jails care home head for sexually assaulting disabled residents - Published A South Korean court has jailed the former head of a disabled care home for sexually assaulting multiple residents, in a case that shocked the nation. The man, surnamed Kim, was handed a 15-year prison term for abusing three residents at the Saekdongwon facility in Incheon City, west of Seoul. The ruling is subject to appeal. Police started investigating Kim after one of his victims, a woman with a severe intellectual disability, came forward in February last year. The case has prompted the government to inspect 1,507 care facilities for disabled people across the country, where 33 cases of suspected abuse were found. South Korean Prime Minister Kim Min-seok had described the abuse at Saekdongwon as "a grave matter that calls into question the very reason for the state's existence". An in-depth assessment of residents commissioned by Ganghwa County found that 20 current and former female residents may have experienced sexual abuse. Many in South Korea have asked how such a case could still occur, especially after laws were strengthened in 2011 to protect people with disabilities from sexual assault. Some have also raised questions on how the director's actions could have gone undetected for so long. Ganghwa County has ordered Saekdongwon to close, while Incheon City officials revoked the licence of the foundation that operated it. However, the closure has been deferred until the remaining residents have been relocated and arrangements for independent living have been completed. item.title: Tiger Woods to change plea after crash arrest
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y7xvpn5kno?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Tiger Woods to change plea after crash arrest - Published Tiger Woods is to change his plea in court five months after he was arrested on a charge of driving under the influence in a rollover crash in Florida. Court records show the change of plea hearing is set for Wednesday morning in Martin County, Florida. The golfer was arrested after the March crash, and had passed a breathalyser test but declined further testing for other drugs. He pleaded not guilty the same month to misdemeanor charges of driving under the influence and refusal to submit to testing. Woods, 50, said he was seeking treatment after the incident. It was not immediately clear what the change of plea would be. The BBC has contacted prosecutors and Woods' attorney. No one was injured in the crash, though Woods had to crawl out through the passenger door to free himself. Police released body camera footage in April that captured the aftermath of the incident, showing the golfing legend after his vehicle clipped a truck and rolled over. In the video, Woods appears calm, kneeling on one knee as he tells officers: "I looked down at my phone, and all of a sudden, boom". He passed a breathalyser test but declined to take a urinalysis screening for other drugs, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said at the time. Woods told officers he had not consumed alcohol that day. When asked about any prescription medication, he responded, "I take a few", adding he had done so earlier that morning. He then listed the medication, though that portion of the footage was redacted. Officers told Woods they suspected his "normal faculties" were impaired by an "unknown substance". Authorities later reported finding two white pills in his pocket, identified as hydrocodone, an opioid commonly prescribed to treat pain. Woods wrote on social media following the incident, "I know and understand the seriousness of the situation I find myself in today. "I am stepping away for a period of time to seek treatment and focus on my health. This is necessary in order for me to prioritise my wellbeing and work toward lasting recovery." The incident marked Woods' second arrest on suspicion of driving under the influence. Related topics - Published28 March

item.title: Guinea-Bissau referendum approves new constitution that expands president's powers
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c93eny4dqp2o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Guinea-Bissau referendum approves new constitution that expands president's powers - Published Voters in Guinea-Bissau have approved a new constitution that significantly expands presidential powers ahead of general elections later this year. The referendum was organised by the military government that seized power in the West African nation last November following a disputed election. Voters have agreed to sweeping reforms allowing the president to appoint and dismiss the prime minister and cabinet, create or abolish ministries and dissolve parliament in the event of a grave political crisis. The main opposition party boycotted the vote, saying the process lacked adequate political and institutional safeguards and threatened the country's transition back to democracy. Guinea-Bissau, one of the poorest countries in the world, has experienced at least nine attempted and successful coups since gaining independence from Portugal in 1974. The UN has dubbed the country a "narco-state" - its coastline has many uninhabited islands, making it ideal for drug traffickers. - Was it a coup or was it a 'sham'? Behind Guinea-Bissau's military takeover - Published3 December 2025 Provisional results announced by the country's electoral commission showed that 70% of voters backed the changes in Sunday's referendum, while 30% voted against them. Turnout was reported at nearly 60%. The new constitution strengthens the presidency at the expense of the prime minister, altering the balance of power under Guinea-Bissau's semi-presidential system. Previously, Guinea-Bissau's legislature appointed a prime minister from the parliamentary majority, who then formed a cabinet - an arrangement the ruling military authorities said had contributed to political instability. The changes now give the president greater authority over the government. However, the five-year presidential term and two-term limit have been retained. The military authorities have argued that the changes are necessary to end repeated disputes between presidents and prime ministers. The new constitution also reduces the number of seats in parliament from 102 to 65 and cuts the number of electoral constituencies from 29 to 12. It introduces new eligibility requirements for presidential candidates, including a provision requiring them to have lived continuously in Guinea-Bissau for the five years before an election. The changes come ahead of presidential and parliamentary elections scheduled for December, which the military authorities say are intended to return the country to civilian rule. But the referendum was strongly opposed by the country's main opposition party, the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), which urged its supporters to boycott the vote. It warned that the changes risked concentrating too much power in the presidency. PAIGC leader Domingos Simões Pereira accused those behind the referendum of seeking to undermine democracy and political freedoms. Some activists told the BBC that the referendum was a mere formality and claimed that 90% of registered voters did not take part. The referendum follows another turbulent period in Guinea-Bissau's politics. The military seized power in November 2025 following a disputed presidential election in which then-President Umaro Sissoco Embaló and opposition candidate Fernando Dias both claimed victory. The junta leaders said they had acted to thwart a plot by unnamed politicians who had "the support of a well-known drug baron" to destabilise the country. The takeover added Guinea-Bissau to a growing list of western and central African countries that have experienced military coups in recent years. December's elections will now be an important test of whether the military authorities follow through on their pledge to restore civilian rule and how the expanded powers of the presidency reshape Guinea-Bissau's fragile political system. item.title: River water smashed into tunnel and chased me for 20 minutes, Nepal worker tells BBC
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cg49590v6k1o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
River water smashed into tunnel and chased me for 20 minutes, Nepal worker tells BBC - Published Nepalese hydropower workers have told the BBC about the catastrophic moment water from the Trishuli River crashed into their tunnel as the region was inundated by deadly flash floods last week. It started with a sudden, strong gust of air, says Pemba Dundu Tamang, whose team of about 30 was constructing the tunnel's concrete lining. The blast of wind sent plywood flying through the air and dislodged heavy machinery. Just outside, houses had already been swept away. "I ran towards the tunnel entrance," he said. "The water was chasing behind me and I was running ahead of it." Tamang lost several family members who were at home at the time. Nepal's death toll has exceeded 1,000 after last week's devastating floods, and officials say about 4,000 are missing. A number of the missing - potentially in the hundreds - are labourers like Tamang, working in a vast network of tunnels at hydropower sites along the river. Engineers have been pumping air into these tunnels as part of a huge rescue operation. "We are focused on search-and-rescue efforts at the tunnels, our work is continuing," Nepal Army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet told AFP news agency. "Our soldiers are also deployed to collect bodies and prevent the spread of disease." The army said 119 people had been rescued on Tuesday. Tamang says he ran for about 20 minutes to flee the violent deluge, which followed him uphill. "I was almost unconscious with shock. I could not think clearly." His colleague, Itha Ghale, says the powerful gust of air almost blew them away as they sprinted. Over 99% of the electricity generated in Nepal comes from hydropower, and Tamang and Ghale had been working at a major production site helping to build the Upper Trishuli 3B Hydropower Project. The plant, which was due to open next year, was designed to re-use water from a hydroelectric plant further upstream to generate additional electricity for Nepal's national grid. There were several different teams operating there - and Tamang says the one operating the large tunnel-lining machine was the last to come out. But soon afterwards came a crushing realisation. "I could see where my house should have been. There was nothing left. That was when I realised everything was gone." Six of Tamang's relatives - his mother, elder brother and sister-in-law and three of their children - are gone, he said. They were at home on the riverside when the floods hit. Only his wife, son and one nephew survived. "I feel life is meaningless now. Surviving feels miserable. I do not know where to eat or where to go," Tamang says. "The dead are at peace. It is those of us who survived who suffer." Ghale, who lost eight members of his family, says he does not know why he survived. "Perhaps it was not my fate to die." The eight family members include his mother and eldest daughter. His three sons and wife survived. Tamang dreads what the future may bring, especially if these hydropower projects are shut down. "If things continue like this, we will go hungry. Sometimes I feel it would have been better not to survive." Tamang ultimately managed to take refuge with a few others in the village of Shanti Bazar for two days until the army came to rescue them. He estimates about 50 to 60 workers were able to escape the tunnel alongside him. He says more people could have been saved if proper resources had been in place. This is echoed by a new report which says there was evidence of growing instability around the glacier in the days before the disaster - and that better early warning systems could have saved lives. Satellite images suggest the glacier surface was moving faster, meltwater was turning brown and a crack was developing in the surrounding rock, according to experts from the Asian Mountain Academic Alliance, the Stimson Centre and China's Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment. These are all possible signs the mountainside was becoming unstable. The avalanche itself moved too fast for conventional warnings to help those closest to it, the scientists say. But further downstream, where the flood took 10 minutes or more to arrive, they say a comprehensive warning system could potentially have saved a significant number of lives. Right now, however, specialists from China, India and Nepal are continuing to use excavators and heavy machinery to blast through debris from the hydropower projects to try to reach workers still trapped at several hydropower sites. "There are probably still some survivors inside. I would be happy if they were rescued quickly," Tamang says. "I know many people who are still trapped there." item.title: Jailed HK activist Joshua Wong pleads guilty to foreign collusion
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2zmzg0408o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Jailed HK activist Joshua Wong pleads guilty to foreign collusion - Published Prominent Hong Kong pro-democracy campaigner Joshua Wong has pleaded guilty to collusion with foreign entities, a charge that carries a maximum sentence of life in prison under Beijing's sweeping National Security Law (NSL). The 29-year-old, who has become the poster child for political activism in Hong Kong, is already serving a sentence of four years and eight months after being convicted of subversion – another NSL violation – in late 2024. The court said Wong would be sentenced at a later date. His earlier jail term is due to end early next year. Wong was at the forefront of the Umbrella Movement in 2014 and massive pro-democracy protests in 2019. The latest charge accuses Wong of conspiring with other campaigners, including exiled activist Nathan Law, to ask foreign countries and entities outside China to impose sanctions or blockades against Beijing. These include activities that took place between July and late November 2020, the court heard. That was the year China introduced the controversial NSL, which critics say has created a climate of fear and quashed dissent in Hong Kong. Beijing and Hong Kong authorities argue the law is necessary to maintain stability and deny it has weakened autonomy. On Tuesday, the court heard that Wong and Law had participated in "international lobbying on numerous occasions", including via visits to the US, Germany and Italy. The duo are among several leaders who founded the pro-democracy party Demosistō in April 2016, and ran for the Hong Kong Legislative Council elections that year. Among other things, prosecutors on Tuesday also accused Wong, along with Law, of promoting the Hong Kong Human Rights and Democracy Act: a US federal law that came into force in November 2019, during Donald Trump's first administration. The Act compels the US government to impose sanctions against mainland China and Hong Kong officials if they are deemed responsible for human rights abuses in Hong Kong. Even after Demosistō disbanded, Wong had maintained that he would not abandon his political stance and would continue to seek support from the international community, the prosecutors said. Wong, dressed in a dark blue shirt and dark-rimmed glasses, did not dispute these allegations. About 40 of Wong's supporters, including fellow activists and some of his close friends, gathered in court on Tuesday. Some shouted: "Hang in there, Joshua!" Wong was seen smiling and nodding in response from the dock. Tsang Kin-shing, a former member of the now-dissolved League of Social Democrats, said he hopes the court will impose a lenient sentence, noting that Wong has by now spent more than 2,000 days in prison. Fellow activist Louis Lee said Wong and his supporters were disheartened that he was handed another NSL charge while already serving time in prison. Wong has continued seeking out new interests while in prison, including learning how to play the guitar and working out. "I hope everyone can learn from him," Lee says. - Published25 June 2019 - Published25 March 2024 - Published30 June 2021

item.title: Germany says Russia behind Leipzig airport drone attack
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5ylm3m67n2o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Germany says Russia behind Leipzig airport drone attack - Published Germany has said Russia was responsible for last month's drone attack at Leipzig's airport. A drone carrying an explosive device was discovered at Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany, close to Ukrainian cargo planes, on 4 August. It failed to explode as the detonator was apparently faulty, and investigators suspect a second drone collided with a cargo aircraft nearby. A third drone was reportedly found near the airport 10 days later. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the Leipzig airport attack followed the "well-established pattern of Russian hybrid operations in Europe" and the assumption was that Germany would be targeted again. Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday accused Germany of planting evidence to blame Moscow for the attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport. Putin did not provide evidence for the accusation. Meanwhile, the Russian embassy in Berlin said the allegation that Russia was responsible was "absurd". Dobrindt said examination of the equipment used along with intelligence findings proved Russian involvement in the attack. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, who was standing beside Dobrindt at a press conference in Berlin, said he would order the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn, and the contract for the Russian House in Berlin will also be terminated - which many observers have said has been used for espionage and to spread Russian propaganda. He also announced tighter entry controls for Russian nationals and vowed to increase pressure on Moscow's shadow fleet - old tankers used by Russia to circumvent Western sanctions following its invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Wadephul said he had summoned Russia's ambassador to Germany, Sergei Nechayev. He was seen arriving at the foreign ministry shortly after the announcement. Maria Zakharova, spokesperson for Russia's foreign ministry, said Moscow would respond in a "mirror-image" fashion to Germany's measures while the Russian embassy described the measures as an "unprecedented escalation in Russian-German relations". "Berlin is sponsoring terrorism", Zakharova told the German Press Agency in reference to its military and economic support provided to Ukraine. There have been previous suggestions that the Goethe-Institut in Moscow would have to cease operations if the Germans went through with closing Russian House. Security experts had speculated that Russia may have been responsible, however Russia has always rejected claims of involvement. Leipzig/Halle Airport in the east of the country is used by Germany's military and Nato allies for the transport of military goods and also serves as a base for Ukraine's Antonov Airlines - which carries most of the country's aerial cargo. The head of Nato, Mark Rutte, said the organisation "stands in full solidarity with Germany". "The evidence is clear. And I welcome the measures announced by Germany in response," he wrote on X. EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on X: "We are united in our resolve to stand against Russian aggression. We will deter anyone who seeks to undermine our freedom and security." She added that the EU was preparing additional sanctions against Russia. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Russia was "escalating tension across the whole region". Polish prosecutors are investigating whether foreign intelligence services were involved in a fire at a factory making drone components on Monday. Meanwhile, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "Russian attempts to undermine our united resolve and our willingness to support Ukraine are futile and doomed to fail." Germany is one of several Nato member states to have reported drone sightings at airports, military and industrial sites over the last year. Berlin has until now been tight-lipped about who may have been behind the Leipzig attack, except to say "foreign powers" may have been involved. US media had already reported that American officials had linked the incident to Russia. Berlin has warned that the country is the "daily target" of hybrid warfare, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned last week that those who carried out hostile acts against Germany would "pay a price". The government is looking to boost the powers of its intelligence services, which have long been criticised as relatively toothless, to counter such threats. Germany is a key backer of Ukraine with Merz forthright in his support for Kyiv. However an MP in Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU) party said the measures so far taken against Russia "fall far short of what is required" and Moscow "just laughs" when its ambassador is summoned. "From a self-proclaimed leading nation, I expect courage and resolve, not self-deterrence and appeasement," said Roderich Kiesewetter. It is not hard to imagine why Ukrainian cargo planes at a key German logistics hub might be in Moscow's sights. But this announcement comes at a delicate moment for Merz's government. A key state election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt could propel the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) into power at a state-level for the first time. The AfD, which is Germany's biggest opposition party, wants to stop sending support to Ukraine and reopen ties with Russia. In a separate development, German police said they were investigating the discovery of improvised explosive and incendiary devices at a power substation in the eastern state of Brandenburg on Tuesday. A power line was damaged, which caused a temporary outage. It is not known who planted the devices. - Published25 August - Published7 August

item.title: Apple Maps renames Lake Ontario as Lake America after Trump order
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cddvyyz0e47o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Apple Maps renames Lake Ontario as Lake America after Trump order - Published Apple has renamed Lake Ontario as Lake America on its Maps app, after an order from US President Donald Trump as part of Washington's trade spat with Canada. The change was made for US-based users, while those in Canada will continue to see Lake Ontario displayed. The BBC has contacted Apple for comment. The iPhone maker's move follows Trump's executive order to change the lake's name after trade talks between the neighbouring countries collapsed late last month, with Washington imposing new 50% tariffs on $20bn (£14.8bn; C$28bn) worth of Canadian goods. Rival technology giant Google made a similar switch for its users in the US in recent days, leading to backlash on social media. Canada has responded to Washington's levies, saying it will implement "dollar for dollar" counter-tariffs. Prime Minister Mark Carney's administration had walked away from the trade negotiations, due to what his office has called unacceptable demands. Carney told the Trump administration to "start being serious" and stop trying to be tough before discussions between the sides can restart. Trump's executive order gives the US Department of the Interior 30 days to update the change with the Geographic Names Information Service - the official database of what places are called in the country. Apple was specifically urged by Trump to rename Lake Ontario on its Maps platform to comply with the executive order signed, according to US Interior Secretary Doug Burgum The president has also posted several AI-generated videos on social media, including a clip of him kicking over a Lake Ontario sign and replacing it with another that says "Welcome to Lake America". At the lake itself, Canada has installed a new sign with the words "Lake Ontario. Now and Always". "Just in case President Trump or anyone else forgets, we've set up this sign to remind them, it's Lake Ontario, now and forever," Ontario Premier Doug Ford said. The names of four of the five Great Lakes - Ontario, Huron, Michigan and Erie - come from indigenous words. Lake Superior was named after an anglicised French word. Lake Ontario, the smallest of the Great Lakes, sits between the Canadian province and the US state of New York. Not all map providers have adopted the new name. MapQuest, a free web mapping service, said "we're not changing it" in a short Facebook post on Friday. The platform rose to the top of the most-downloaded free applications earlier this week on the Canadian Apple App Store. Last week, Google said in a blog post that it had changed the name on its Maps service for US-based users. The Maps app is updated to "reflect name changes in official government sources", meaning that users in the US will see Lake America while those in Canada will see Lake Ontario, Google said. The company made a similar decision in 2025 to re-designate the Gulf of Mexico after Trump declared it would be called the Gulf of America. Google was sued by Mexico over allegedly ignoring the country's requests not to rename the Gulf for US users. Apple also changed the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America on its maps service for US users. Related topics - Published2 days ago - Published11 February 2025

item.title: Ariana Grande makes emotional tour exit and steps back from public life
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4gj0l34g78o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Ariana Grande makes emotional tour exit and steps back from public life - Published Ariana Grande made an emotional exit on Tuesday night, as she wrapped up her Eternal Sunshine tour, and prepared to step back from public life. The singer was occasionally close to tears - most notably during One Last Time, the song that took on extra meaning as an anthem for survivors of the 2017 Manchester terror attack. "London, I'm going to need you to help me on this one," she said, kneeling down to be near the audience throughout the performance. Last month, Grande announced a break from all future public-facing appearances following months of intense speculation about her health and appearance. The step-back includes Grande's withdrawal from a production of Stephen Sondheim's Sunday in the Park with George at London's Barbican next summer. She was due to appear alongside her Wicked co-star Jonathan Bailey. He also pulled out of the production on Tuesday. On stage in London, Grande showed no signs of fragility or poor health - other than a foot injury that required her to swap her trademark stilettos for a succession of knee-high platform boots. Nonetheless, she sprang across the stage in sync with her dancers, often on tip-toe to compensate for the lost height of her high heels. But her voice faltered again during the song Nowhere, Nobody, as she sang the line: "Hard to believe in a perfect ending." The blip was short-lived, though. Professional to the core, Grande regained her composure and was never less than magnetic on stage. Addressing the audience towards the end of the show, the singer thanked fans for their support. "This has been one of the most beautiful extraordinary experiences of my life and I just wanted to express my gratitude without sobbing completely," she said. "I'll cherish this experience always. I have the best fans in the entire world and I always have. Thank you for all of your effort and continuing to make this so special. "I have loved every minute of this with you all and I just wanted to make sure I express how grateful I am." ‘Boundaries need to be set’ Grande announced her hiatus last month, shortly after releasing the music video for her latest single, Petal, which led some fans to express concern about her weight. One wrote on X that the 33-year-old had "become so thin that people are genuinely concerned". Two days later, Grande's publicist announced her "step back from visibility", due to "endless, ongoing public scrutiny". Speaking to People magazine, a source close to the singer noted that she "performs a very physical show... healthily and successfully at a very high level night after night". Grande herself moved to reassure fans the following night, saying her decision came from a "thoughtful, empowered place", and had been planned "a long time ago". "I heard my fans were worried negativity was ruining things for me but... that could not be more than the opposite," she said on stage in Chicago. "Boundaries need to be set, human beings do need a break sometimes." Even before that announcement, Grande had described the Eternal Sunshine tour - which started in the US in June - as "one last hurrah", saying she wanted to take more acting roles after her Oscar-nominated performance in Wicked. That meant her 10 show residency at London's O2 Arena represented many fans' last chance to see her in concert. They flew in from all over the world - from China and Australia and cities all across Europe - with 200,000 people attending the London dates alone. On the second night, Grande surprised the audience by bringing out her Wicked co-star Cynthia Erivo for a rendition of their movie duet For Good. Across the board, reviews were positive. "There's no question about it - Ariana Grande is one of the best singers of her generation," wrote Rolling Stone magazine, external, noting that "there were no signs" of the singer "struggling or not wanting to be there". The Telegraph called the show "flawless", external, praising its "Hollywood-indebted" staging, and Grande's "genuine affection for Britain". My own review highlighted quieter songs like Imperfect For You felt delicate and gorgeous and strangely intimate in a room of 20,000 people. But Guardian writer Kate Solomon said she was "gripped by genuine concern", external for Grande, even when she was enjoying the show, adding: "I really hope this tour does not go down in history for the wrong reasons". The NME, by contrast, was left breathless by the star's physical prowess. "Throughout the show," marvelled Nick Levine, external, "she skips across the stage in skyscraper heels that most drag performers would baulk at." That wasn't the case on the final night, however, due to what Grande described as a "deep cut" on her foot. Writing on Instagram, she assured fans the injury wasn't serious, insisting she was "on the mend" and would complete her final shows "even if I am a few inches shorter than usual". She did so with a huge smile spread across her face, leaning into the big notes of Dangerous Woman, and sprinting across the stage during Break Free - one of many up-tempo highlights. She ended the show as she always does - attached to a harness, ascending into the rafters of the O2 and disappearing. Fans were left wondering when, if ever, they'd see her perform again. Among them was Rachid, a London fan who said he was "devastated" by Grande's withdrawal from touring. "That's why I really, really wanted to come to the last show because I was like, 'What if she never comes back?'" he said. "So that's why I was here - to enjoy everything she has to give us, and hopefully she gets a nice break now." "I'm not gonna lie, I'd do the same thing," joked Manchester fan Nadine. "Like, I made my money, got on stage, sang my heart out... I'd bugger off, too! Straight to Hawaii, or somewhere else where nobody knows who I am, you know what I mean?" Lukas, who’d travelled from France for the concert said it was good to see Grande taking matters into her own hands. "She's said goodbye and now she's gonna rest for her safety," he said. "If she needs the break, she takes it and we, the real fans, understand." "It's sad that people are speculating about someone else's health," said Polish fan Alejandro Grande (no relation, he insisted). "And it's sad that she has to make a decision for herself just to reclaim her power and her energy." "Yeah, it's completely up to her," agreed Bella Hopkins from Bronsgrove. "I think people should respect how she feels and what she needs." Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.
